title: The Ragmala
hook: the Granth's last page is a garland of raga names, and Sikhs hold more than one view of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Jaijavanti: it's passing, it's passing. Your line was before it slips by. What did you start today instead of later? A new week begins. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

Two families sit down to the same holiday meal, and one says the blessing one way, and the other another way, and both have done it like that for as long as anyone remembers. Nobody leaves the table. The food is shared. The difference is just there, spoken plainly, held kindly. Sikhs have a page like that. It's the very last page of the Guru Granth Sahib as it is printed, and it's called the Ragmala. Sikhs don't all read it the same way. Today: the page, the difference, and how the Panth holds it.
screen: `TWO WAYS AT ONE TABLE.` → `THE LAST PAGE OF THE GRANTH.` → `HOW A DIFFERENCE IS HELD.`

segments.voice: First, the page itself. After the last raga, Jaijavanti, come collections of verses, and then Guru Arjan's Mundavani, which tradition calls the seal on the book, where he says the dish holds truth, contentment and reflection. Then, in the printed Granth, one more page: the Ragmala. The name is usually read as a garland of ragas, and that's what it looks like. It's a list in verse, naming ragas and arranging them in families, with the ragas set alongside related melodies. It reads like a garland of music names, strung together. Here is the difference. Some Sikhs hold that the Ragmala belongs to the Granth as it was handed on, and recite it at the close of a complete reading. Other Sikhs hold that it was added later, that it isn't Gurbani, the Gurus' word, and they close the reading at the Mundavani instead. Both are Sikhs, devoted to the same Guru Granth Sahib. Now the Panth's own answer. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Panth's code of conduct, doesn't silence either side. In paraphrase, it says a full reading may be concluded with the Mundavani or with the Ragmala, according to the custom of the place, and it notes that the Panth holds differing views. It also says no copy of the Granth should be written or printed without the Ragmala. So the code keeps the page in every copy, and the question stays open, and the community goes on sitting at one table. Not every difference has to be settled to be lived with. Your line: differ with respect.
screen: `MUNDAVANI: THE SEAL ON THE BOOK.` · `A GARLAND OF RAGA NAMES.` · `SOME RECITE IT; SOME CLOSE BEFORE IT.` · `THE PAGE STAYS IN EVERY COPY.` · then, large: `DIFFER WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the page, respectfully. If you can, open the last page of the Granth online and let your eyes move slowly over the names of the ragas, many of which you've now met. Read it the way you'd read a family tree at someone else's home: with interest, and with care. You don't need to decide anything. Then sit, and bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters. Let the breath stay even. Hold the difference and the person side by side, without letting go of either. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for a kind heart toward them. If you don't, simply notice that both can be held at once. The bell holds the time.
Ragmala. The garland of ragas on the Granth's last printed page; some Sikhs recite it, some close the reading before it, and the Rehat Maryada leaves the closing to each place's custom. Today's word.
Your line: differ with respect. Today, when you disagree with someone, say the difference plainly once, and then keep sitting at the table. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: At the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, some congregations recite the Ragmala and others conclude with the Mundavani, following the custom of the place, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada allows.
